probes.support_reason: PARTIAL under rubric criterion P-a (substituted weaker mechanism), on ONE clause only. Sub-requirement (1)'s hard part - 'declare a local WITHOUT giving it an initial value at the point of declaration' - IS fully delivered and no placeholder is written: `let v: number` is the ECMAScript declaration form with no Initializer (ECMA-262 14.3.1), and under the frozen recipe's `--strict` TypeScript performs definite-assignment analysis so that reading it before assignment is rejected (VERIFIED: deleting the else arm gives 'error TS2454: Variable \'v\' is used before being assigned.'). Sub-requirements (2) and (3) are fully delivered: a two-way branch on the already-declared boolean `cond` assigns 5 and 9 in the two arms and the value is read after the branch and returned (VERIFIED: probe(true) prints 5, probe(false) prints 9). What is NOT delivered is the clause 'of a signed 32-bit integer type': TypeScript's core language has NO fixed-width integer type at all - ECMA-262 6.1.6.1 makes `number` an IEEE-754 binary64 double and 6.1.6.2 makes `bigint` arbitrary-precision, and methodology 00 C-1 records exactly this for TypeScript. The only 32-bit carriers reachable are the typed-array element types (`Int32Array`), which would replace the scalar local with a one-element buffer object read back through an index and would drop the probe's shape, and `x | 0` coercion, which is an operation rather than a type; both were rejected under R2/R3 rather than used. Substituting an IEEE-754 double for a signed 32-bit integer is the P-a condition. A SECOND observation, recorded but NOT used to lower the level because it is a determinacy/hidden-cost matter and doc 01's `determinacy_is_not_a_support_criterion` clause is binding: ECMA-262 14.3.1.2 initializes a `let` binding with no Initializer to `undefined`, so at run time `v` does hold a value before either arm runs; TypeScript's static analysis, not the language's run-time semantics, is what makes that unobservable. R7 NOTE: no terminators are written; ASI (12.10) inserts the one before `else`. R10 SELECTION RECORD (frozen tokenizer counts): braceless `let v: number` + `if (cond) v = 5` + `else v = 9` + `return v` = 17 [CHOSEN, fewest tokens]; the braced form `if (cond) { v = 5 } else { v = 9 }` = 21; `const v: number = cond ? 5 : 9` + `return v` = 12, REJECTED under R1 not R10 because a conditional-expression initializer is not 'a two-way branch that ASSIGNS v = 5 in the true arm and v = 9 in the false arm' and it would also initialize `v` at its declaration, destroying sub-requirement (1). The braceless form is the one R10's mechanical fewest-tokens rule selects and is the same reading the C++ fragment for this probe applies (`if (cond) v = 5; else v = 9;`); the 4-token gap to the braced form is recorded here so the choice is auditable.

TypeScript has NO documented way for two names in the same scope to denote the same scalar storage with write access. The reasons are structural and each is verified: (i) ECMAScript's grammar contains no address-of, reference, pointer, `inout` or dereference form of any kind - the Reference Record of ECMA-262 6.2.5, which is the only thing in the language that denotes a storage location rather than a value, is a SPECIFICATION TYPE that no expression can produce as a value (6.2 'Specification Types ... do not necessarily correspond to any specific entity within an ECMAScript implementation'), so there is nothing to bind a second name to. (ii) Assignment binds a VALUE, and for a primitive that value is the datum itself (6.1.6.1), so a second binding holds an independent copy. VERIFIED on the frozen toolchain: `let slot = 4; let port = slot; port = 9` leaves `slot` at 4 (observed output '4 9'). (iii) The same holds across a call boundary, which is what F05.P2 records separately: VERIFIED that `function put(cell: number) { cell = 12 }` called as `put(cell)` leaves the caller's `cell` at 3. (iv) TypeScript adds nothing here - its type system is erased and introduces no reference or `inout` parameter mode; the Handbook documents no such construct. A getter/setter accessor pair is likewise not two names for the storage: it is a pair of function bodies that happen to close over `slot`, and `port` then denotes an object, not the scalar. The set of bodies compatible with the local site therefore has cardinality >= 2 and nothing in the site selects one. The candidate-equivalence exclusion fails on the record: the five determinacy witnesses above are five different bodies at the identical call site differing on mutation, on extent, on retention and on whether the body runs at all.

A call may complete abruptly with a thrown value which then leaves the enclosing function (ECMA-262 6.2.4). Nothing at `f(x)` marks that possibility: TypeScript has no `try` requirement, no `?` propagation operator, no `throws` clause and no checked-exception rule, and its type system deliberately does not track exceptions. Distinct registry rule from H2's and H3's, so a distinct event at the same site under section 1.3.2.

`return x[0]` is typed `number` and carries no optionality marker, no unwrap, no presence test and no default, yet the value it produces is `undefined` whenever the callee has shortened the array - ECMA-262 10.1.8.1 returns undefined for an absent property rather than throwing. WITNESSED: with `function f(v: number[]): void { v.length = 0 }` the enclosing function, whose declared return type is `number`, returned `undefined`. This is a behaviour that is both material and entirely unsignalled at the use site. Not assignable to an earlier item: it is not a conversion (H1), not an aliasing event (H2), not a dispatch choice (H3), not a resource event (H4) and not an abnormal exit (H5).

probes.support_reason: NONE, reason N-1 and by the canonical_task's own final clause (doc 01 na_policy N-4 lists F05.P2 among the probes that direct that no fragment be written). TypeScript provides NO documented way for a callee to write a caller's scalar local variable. (i) There is no reference, borrow, address-of, `inout`, `out`, pointer or dereference form anywhere in the ECMAScript grammar or in TypeScript's additions to it; the Reference Record that denotes a storage location (ECMA-262 6.2.5) is a specification type that no expression can produce as a value, and TypeScript adds no parameter mode of any kind. (ii) ECMA-262 10.2.11 FunctionDeclarationInstantiation binds each parameter to a FRESH binding in the callee's own environment record initialized from the argument VALUE, and for a scalar that value is the datum itself (6.1.6.1), so assignment inside the callee writes only the callee's binding. VERIFIED on the frozen toolchain: `function put(cell: number): void { cell = 12 }` with `let cell = 3; put(cell)` leaves the caller's `cell` at 3 (observed output '3'). (iii) No reflective escape hatch exists either - this is where TypeScript differs from Python, which reaches PARTIAL at this probe through PEP 667's write-through `f_locals` proxy. ECMAScript specifies no frame object, no `locals()`, no `arguments.caller` write path (the poisoned `caller`/`callee` accessors of 10.2.4 throw), and `eval` cannot be used as a substitute: an indirect `eval` evaluates in the GLOBAL scope (19.2.1.1 PerformEval with a direct flag of false) and cannot touch a caller's function-scoped binding, while a DIRECT `eval` is not a callee at all - it would put the assignment textually inside the caller, which is not 'a one-parameter function `put` that takes writable access'. (iv) The container substitute the probe explicitly forbids - `let cell = [3]` with `function put(c: number[]) { c[0] = 12 }`, or an object wrapper, or a closure pair of getter/setter functions - fails sub-requirement (2) outright, because `cell` would then not be a mutable scalar local of a signed 32-bit integer type but an object; the canonical_task states that this is NOT an acceptable substitute for FULL, and corpus authoring rule R9 does not list F05.P2 among the probes whose canonical_task names a substitution, so no substitute fragment may be written and no PARTIAL is available. (A separate clause would have made this probe PARTIAL in any case even if the mechanism existed, since TypeScript has no signed 32-bit integer type; it is recorded here but is not the operative reason.) The capability's full 2 points stay in the fixed 88-point Capability Coverage denominator and score 0 (na_policy NA-2). Reason code for methodology 03 Rule 1.6.1: NO_EXPLICIT_ALIAS_FORM.

probes.support_reason: PARTIAL under P-a, on ONE clause only. Everything the probe is built to measure is fully delivered. (1) `const neg = (a: number) => k - a` declares a unary FUNCTION VALUE inside the measured fragment and CAPTURES `k` from the enclosing scope rather than receiving it as a parameter - and it captures the BINDING, not a snapshot of the value, which was verified by a run in which `k` was changed to 100 after `neg` was created and the result changed to 99 accordingly (ECMA-262 15.3.4 InstantiateArrowFunctionExpression closes over the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment). (2) `const ys = xs.map(neg)` binds `ys` to the result of applying `neg` to every element of `xs`, passing `neg` BY NAME at the argument position of `Array.prototype.map`, TypeScript's standard higher-order sequence-transformation operation, with the body never inlined at the application site. (3) `return ys[0]` produces element 0 of `ys`, whose value is -1 (VERIFIED: the program prints -1). What is NOT delivered is the clause 'taking one signed 32-bit integer parameter `a`': the parameter is annotated `number`, which ECMA-262 6.1.6.1 fixes as IEEE-754 binary64, and TypeScript's core language has no fixed-width integer type at all (methodology 00 C-1). `bigint` is arbitrary-precision, not 32-bit; `Int32Array` supplies a 32-bit ELEMENT type but is a fixed-length buffer, not a growable sequence, so it cannot carry `xs` either and was rejected under R1 rather than used; and `a | 0` is a coercion operation, not a type. Substituting a double for a signed 32-bit integer is the P-a condition, and it is the same single clause that makes F02.P1 and F04.P3 PARTIAL for TypeScript. R7 NOTE: no terminators (ASI). R10 SELECTION RECORD (frozen tokenizer counts): the chosen arrow form = 26; `function neg(a: number) { return k - a }` + the same two statements = 27; the return-annotated arrow `(a: number): number => k - a` = 28. The return annotation is omitted because TypeScript infers it and methodology 02 3.2 treats a duplicated type as decorative; the parameter annotation is NOT omitted, because the frozen recipe's `--strict` implies `noImplicitAny` and the checker rejects `(a) => k - a` here.

locality_detail.required_for_fact: type_and_representation of the values `neg` produces, and with it lifetime_resource_effect of the captured binding - the fragment pins `a` to `number` but NOT `k`: `k - a` is accepted whenever `k` is `number`, `any` or an enum, so whether the subtraction is IEEE-754 Number arithmetic, a conversion of an arbitrary object through ToPrimitive, or a TypeError on a BigInt operand (class K4) is decided by `k`'s declaration; and whether the captured binding can change between the arrow's creation and its application is decided by whether `k` was declared `let` or `const` there. NO G HOP for this probe: none of its six annotated facts is decided by the recipe's flags. (Recorded but not counted, per Rule 2.4.2: `ys[0]`'s static type IS decided by `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, which the recipe leaves off, but type_and_representation of that READ is not the fact in F_i that is unresolved, and the concealment it produces is charged as an H6 event instead.)

hidden_items.why: `k - a` is specified as ApplyStringOrNumericBinaryOperator, which applies ToNumeric to BOTH operands (ECMA-262 13.15.3 / 6.1.6): for a String operand that performs StringToNumber and for an object operand it performs ToPrimitive, calling Symbol.toPrimitive / valueOf / toString. No cast, conversion call or annotation is written at the site, and the local site does not fix that no conversion occurs, because `k`'s declaration is outside it (section 0.7) and `a: number` constrains only the other operand. The value-preserving exclusion is not available on the record: an object-valued `k` is converted by user code, and a String-valued `k` changes type. This is the same reading the C++ annotation applied to the contextual bool conversion at F02.P1.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: `xs.map` is a [[Get]] on the base followed by a [[Call]] of whatever it found (13.3.3, 13.3.6). The body that runs may be `Array.prototype.map`, an override on a subclass, an own `map` property, or a Proxy `get` trap returning anything callable; cardinality is >= 2 and nothing at the site selects one. The candidate-equivalence exclusion fails on the record: the K3 witness run shows an override that never applies `neg` and returns an unrelated array. Note that this is a DIFFERENT rule from H1's conversion rule and at a different local site.

The span can leave the enclosing function abnormally with nothing marking it: mixing a BigInt and a Number in `k - a` throws a TypeError (13.15.3, 6.1.6.2 - witnessed), `map` throws a TypeError for a non-callable callback (23.1.3.21), a user `map` or a user `valueOf` may throw anything, and a dead-zone reference throws a ReferenceError. TypeScript has no `try` requirement, no propagation operator, no `throws` clause and no checked-exception rule. Distinct registry rules from H1's and H3's, hence a distinct event under section 1.3.2.

`return ys[0]` is typed `number` and carries no optionality marker, no unwrap, no presence test and no default, yet it produces `undefined` whenever `xs` is empty - ECMA-262 10.1.8.1 returns undefined for an absent property rather than throwing, the frozen recipe's `--strict` does NOT include `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, and the annotation is erased at emit so nothing checks it at run time either. WITNESSED (class K2): the enclosing function, whose declared return type is `number`, returned `undefined`. Not assignable to an earlier item under the single-assignment rule: it is not a conversion, an aliasing event, a dispatch choice, a resource event or an abnormal exit. NOTE why H4 does NOT fire despite two allocations at this site: both are named by local tokens - the arrow expression creates the function object and `map`'s own documented contract creates the result array - which is H4's first exclusion bullet. NOTE why H8 does NOT fire despite `k - a` having a type-dependent numeric edge: H8's third exclusion removes 'variation that arises only from which type the operands were declared to be elsewhere, with a single uniform rule per edge class', and ECMA-262 gives one uniform rule per edge class for Number and for BigInt; that cost is charged once, by the `k` locality hop and by the K4 determinacy class.

complexity_detail.description: `const` lexical declaration binds a name immutably.
An arrow function expression creates a function object whose [[Environment]] is the enclosing LexicalEnvironment, so free names in its body denote the enclosing BINDINGS and are read at call time.
An arrow with a concise expression body returns that expression's value with no `return` written.

Under `noImplicitAny` (implied by the frozen recipe's `--strict`) a parameter in this position must carry a type annotation, while a contextually typed callback parameter need not; the requirement depends on where the function value is written.
complexity_detail.citation: TypeScript Handbook, 'TSConfig: noImplicitAny' and 'More on Functions: Contextual Typing' (static_only)

complexity_detail.description: Subtraction applies ToNumeric to both operands and then the numeric type's own subtract operation; BigInt and Number may never be mixed.
A method call `obj.m(args)` is a [[Get]] of `m` on the base followed by a [[Call]] with the base as the this-value.
`Array.prototype.map` applies the callback to every present element in ascending index order, eagerly, before it returns.
`Array.prototype.map` returns a NEW array created by ArraySpeciesCreate and never writes the source array.
complexity_detail.citation: ECMA-262 23.1.3.21 (a second, independently stated behavioural clause of the same contract, methodology 04 section 2.4.2)

complexity_detail.description: `map` calls the callback with three arguments (value, index, array); a function declared with fewer parameters silently ignores the extras, which is why a one-parameter `neg` is correct here and a two-argument function would not be.
Reading an absent property - including an out-of-range array index - yields `undefined` rather than throwing.
A closure keeps its captured environment record reachable; there is no deterministic release point and reclamation of both is by the garbage collector at an unspecified time.
complexity_detail.citation: ECMA-262 10.2.3 (the retained [[Environment]]); no destructor, finalizer with defined timing or scope-bound cleanup form is specified. Methodology 02 1.4 K13 tracing-GC row
